title: Pressure and urgency
description: Audio, video, and phone calls are now part of the scam. The more someone tries to rush you, the more it matters to stop and verify.

events.message: 'I need you to approve a transfer RIGHT NOW, I'm in a meeting, I'll explain later.' — message from your manager.

emails.subject: Urgent confirmation - PIX transfer for the acquisition
emails.bodyHtml:
Attached is the screenshot from our video call just now confirming the details.

Please make the PIX transfer of R$48,000 to the key below today. This is confidential until the official announcement of the acquisition on Friday.

PIX key: 45.812.finance@fastpay.com.br

internalDbRecord.notes: 'leroymerlin.corp-mail.com' is not a company domain — it's a subdomain of 'corp-mail.com,' a third-party service.

outOfBandCheck.channelDescription: Call to CFO Carla Mendes's registered extension
outOfBandCheck.details: The CFO confirmed that no video call took place and that there is no acquisition underway.

aiAssistantHint.reasoning: The formal wording and the attached image appear legitimate. The AI doesn't analyze video/audio or verify identity through other means.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'leroymerlin.corp-mail.com' is a subdomain of 'corp-mail.com' — a third-party service, not the company.
This sender has never been used before to communicate with the company.
The real CFO, contacted by phone, confirmed that neither the video call nor the acquisition exists.

explanation.short: Subdomain trick + fabricated video call image to lend credibility to a PIX request.
explanation.detailed: 'leroymerlin.corp-mail.com' looks like it has 'leroymerlin' in the name, but the real address is 'corp-mail.com' — the company shows up only as decoration, to fool a quick reader. The attached 'confirmation' is just an image, easy to fake. An urgent, secret transfer request that bypasses the normal process is the fake-payment scam in a boss's name. The only real defense is to confirm through another channel, like calling the number you already have for the person.

emails.subject: [Alert] Your Microsoft 365 account has been compromised
emails.bodyHtml:
We detected suspicious activity on your corporate Microsoft 365 account.

To protect your data, call our specialized technical support now: 0800 025 1188, or install our remote access tool so we can resolve this with you immediately.

internalDbRecord.notes: Microsoft never asks you to install remote access tools by email, nor does it offer support via this kind of toll-free number.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'microsoft-0365support.com' does not belong to Microsoft — it's a third-party domain created to imitate official support.
The link directly downloads a 'remote access tool' executable.
Microsoft never requests the installation of remote access tools by email.

explanation.short: Fake Microsoft technical support requesting the installation of remote access.
explanation.detailed: This 'fake tech support' scam combines a scary alert (compromised account) with an apparently convenient solution (a call or a tool) that, in reality, gives the attacker full control of the computer. Legitimate technology companies never ask you to install remote access tools from an unsolicited email — if there's real doubt about the account's security, the right path is to go directly to the official website, without clicking anything in the email.

emails.subject: Your two-step verification code
emails.bodyHtml:
Hello,

We received a login attempt on your corporate account from a new device.

If this was you, use the code 482913 to confirm access. If you don't recognize this attempt, ignore this email and your account will remain secure.

internalDbRecord.notes: Company's official domain, internal authentication system.

investigationHints.summaryText: It comes from the company's official address, spelled correctly, with no swapped letters.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass — the email really did come from the company's official infrastructure.

explanation.short: A real two-step verification alert, from the official address, with a safe option to ignore it.
explanation.detailed: Unlike a scam, this email doesn't ask you to click anything or rush you. It just gives a code and explains what to do if you don't recognize the sign-in. The address and the email's checks confirm it's real. A real two-step verification alert works like this: it informs, has no link, and gives a safe way out for anyone who doesn't recognize the sign-in.

emails.subject: Fwd: Fwd: OPPORTUNITY - payroll loan approved
emails.bodyHtml:
Good morning everyone, I got this in the company WhatsApp group and it's being forwarded to everybody, here's the link:

Payroll loan approved with no credit check, approval in 5 minutes, click to see your exclusive employee terms.

investigationHints.summaryText: The link leads to a random financial-scam address, unrelated to any real bank.
Sent from a personal Hotmail account forwarding a chain message, not from an official HR channel.

explanation.short: Financial scam chain message forwarded through a personal email, with no specific target within the company.
explanation.detailed: This is a classic mass scam — 'easy loan, no credit check' is a generic lure that circulates through WhatsApp groups and gets forwarded, often by well-meaning people who didn't notice the scam. Unlike the previous attacks, this one wasn't specifically targeted at the company nor does it use Leroy Merlin infrastructure — there's no need to involve IT, but it also shouldn't be forwarded any further. The right move here is simply to delete it.

emails.subject: Updated invoice - new payee starting this month
emails.bodyHtml:
Dear all,

We would like to inform you that, due to a corporate restructuring, our payments will now be received under a new company name. Please find the updated invoice attached with the new bank details.

internalDbRecord.notes: Legitimate vendor account, but no corporate restructuring was previously communicated through official channels.

outOfBandCheck.channelDescription: Call to Vendor ABC's already-known finance contact
outOfBandCheck.details: The vendor confirmed that no restructuring took place and that their email account was recently compromised.

investigationHints.summaryText: No corporate restructuring was previously communicated through official channels — a payee change with no advance notice is a red flag.
The vendor confirmed by phone that their email account was compromised and that no restructuring took place.

explanation.short: The vendor's real account was compromised to swap the invoice's bank details.
explanation.detailed: This is the 'swapped invoice' scam at its worst: the email really does come from the vendor's real account (which is why the checks pass), because the account was hacked. A change of payment account, with no notice through the usual channel, is always a reason to confirm outside of email before paying. It was that confirmation that exposed the scam.

emails.subject: 🎉 EXCLUSIVE COUPON: 70% OFF today only for employees!
emails.bodyHtml: Congratulations! You've been selected for an exclusive 70% discount coupon at our partner store. Valid only for the next 2 hours.

investigationHints.summaryText: A random scam-ad address ('mega-descontos-vip.shop'), with no connection to the company.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all fail — typical of mass spam sent from disposable infrastructure.

explanation.short: Generic promotional spam with artificial urgency, with no specific target.
explanation.detailed: Pressure ('only for the next 2 hours') and an offer too good to be true are the face of a scam blasted out in bulk, to any email list, with no connection to the company. It isn't a targeted attack that needs IT. The right move here is simply to delete it.
